question.text:
Determine which of the following is the graph of $x=\dfrac{2\sqrt y +8}{y^{3/2}} \,$ by completing the following table:

$y$ $1$ $4$ $9$ $16$
$x$ $ $ $ $ $ $ $ $
question.explanation:
To graph this curve, we can start by calculating the value of $x$ for various values of $y,$ as follows:

\begin{align} y=1 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x= \dfrac{2\sqrt 1 +8}{1^{3/2}} = 10 \\[5pt] y=4 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x= \dfrac{2\sqrt 4 +8}{4^{3/2}}= \dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] y=9 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x= \dfrac{2\sqrt 9 +8}{9^{3/2}} = \dfrac{14}{27} \\[5pt] y=16 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x =\dfrac{2\sqrt {16} +8}{16^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{4} \\[5pt] \end{align}

We can summarize these results in the following table:

$y$ $1$ $4$ $9$ $16$
$x$ $10$ $\dfrac{3}{2}$ $\dfrac{14}{27}$ $\dfrac{1}{4}$

So, we have the following points:

\[ (10,1), \quad \left(\dfrac{3}{2},4\right), \quad \left(\dfrac{14}{27},9\right), \quad \left(\dfrac{1}{4},16\right). \]

question.text:
Determine which of the following is the graph of $x= (2y +1)^2 -6\,$ by completing the following table:

$y$ $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ $0$ $1$ $\dfrac{3}{2}$
$x$ $ $ $ $ $ $ $ $
question.explanation:
To graph this curve, we can start by calculating the value of $x$ for various values of $y,$ as follows:

\begin{align} y=-\dfrac{1}{2} & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x= \left[2\cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) +1\right]^2 -6 = -6 \\[5pt] y=0 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x= (2\cdot 0 +1)^2 -6 = -5 \\[5pt] y=1 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x= (2\cdot 1 +1)^2 -6 = 3 \\[5pt] y=\dfrac{3}{2} & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x = \left[2\cdot \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) +1\right]^2 -6 = 10 \\[5pt] \end{align}

We can summarize these results in the following table:

$y$ $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ $0$ $1$ $\dfrac{3}{2}$
$x$ $-6$ $-5$ $3$ $10$

So, we have the following points:

\[ \left(-6,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right), \quad (-5,0), \quad (3,1), \quad \left(10,\dfrac{3}{2}\right). \]

If we plot these points and connect them with a smooth curve, we get the following graph:
